content: Pus is a thick, whitish-yellow or yellow fluid that forms as a result of the body’s inflammatory response to infection, particularly in cases involving pyogenic (pus-forming) bacteria. When pus accumulates in a confined tissue space, it is referred to as an abscess. If the pus collects visibly beneath or within the epidermis, it is termed a pustule or pimple. The formation of pus occurs due to the activity of white blood cells, both living and dead, which migrate to the site of infection. Substances or conditions that lead to the production of pus are described as suppurative, pyogenic, or purulent. If both mucus and pus are produced, the term mucopurulent is used. Pus is composed of a protein-rich fluid called liquor puris and dead neutrophils, which are a type of white blood cell integral to the body’s innate immune defense. Neutrophils are generated in the bone marrow and released into the bloodstream. When an infection is detected, neutrophils are directed to the site of infection through a process called chemotaxis, which is typically initiated by cytokines released from macrophages that have identified invading pathogens. Upon reaching the site of infection, neutrophils engulf and destroy bacteria. After fulfilling their role, the neutrophils die and are subsequently broken down by macrophages through phagocytosis. The resulting material, composed of these dead neutrophils, forms the viscous substance known as pus. Neutrophils are the most abundant type of leukocyte (white blood cell) in human blood, accounting for approximately 40% to 75% of all leukocytes. The presence of pus in a wound or on dry skin is a clear indication of infection and necessitates cleaning with an antiseptic to prevent further complications. Although pus is typically whitish-yellow in color, its appearance can vary depending on the underlying infection. For example, infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa may produce blue pus due to the bacterial pigment pyocyanin. Amoebic abscesses in the liver can result in brownish pus. Pus may also appear reddish if it becomes mixed with blood. Additionally, pus can emit an odor, which may vary depending on the type of infection and the bacteria involved.
